It's also expected that there will be fewer postdoc positions and in turn more staff scientists (which is supposedly preferable as those positions are more stable).

Good news, but damn.. It just makes you think. Postdoc work has more educational and knowledge requirements than just about any job there is. And a healthy number of these postdocs are working on some of the most important projects for the furtherment of society. And they work ridiculous hours. And get paid an average of 45k. What has our socioeconomic system turned into? Instead of rewarding merit or even hard work, we reward who's willing to play the scummiest to get their dollars. There are some exceptions, but they are indeed the exceptions to the rule.

Supply and demand. Lots of people want to be a researcher into obscure subjects, not many people want to pay them to do it. Your pay isn't a function of how much education you have, it's how much people want what you produce.

And this is terrible news if you're someone going for such a position: The government just reduced your value even further.

This definitely isn't going to hurt people going for such a position. That would only be true if we were at anything like an equilibrium between the value provided by postdocs and their compensation offered. Eg - if a post doc only offers $50k of value and a regulation states that they must be paid $55k then yeah, institutions are going to make do with fewer postdocs. But that's not even close to the case. Postdocs, at least in the 'real' sciences, are going to generate value far in excess of their compensation.

Like in most industries in the US there is a wide discrepancy between compensation offered and the value created by an employee. In other words companies aren't paying $x because that price is commensurate with the value produced by said employee. They're paying $x because they can get people to work for them for $x by taking advantage of the fact that individuals cannot simply choose to not work. Working against this, postdocs in various regional locations have managed to unionize and easily negotiated far more favorable, yet clearly still mutually beneficial, contracts and conditions.

In the United States our economic system is falling apart I think in large part because of something directly related to this. The proportion of people needed to maintain production across all industries in in decline as worker productivity increases at the same time, as you mention, that there are more qualified applicants for just about every position than ever before. This would be a bad situation if employers were offering value-commensurate wages, but it's made even worse by the fact that they're not. If WalMart could pay in rice, beans, and water - they probably would. And they'd still have piles of applications. This myopic behavior is accelerating the necessity of change. It's as if these companies don't realize their customers are the very people they're marginalizing. In many ways it's akin to a tragedy of the commons. Companies just want to maximize their own revenue, but they're not considering the sustainability of their source of revenue.
